dedupe_keys.name: voluntary relocation of flood exposed households in the eferdinger becken upper austria climate adapt

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the voluntary resettlement of households from the Eferdinger Becken on the Danube in Upper Austria, one of the country's most flood-prone areas, after major floods in 1991, 1997, 2002 and 2013. A cost-benefit analysis found relocation the most cost-efficient option, and a zone of 154 properties was mapped with residents and civil protection. The page reports a EUR 250 million budget for flood protection and resettlement agreed with the federal government, plus EUR 75 million of regional funding, with costs shared 50% federal, 30% provincial and 20% owner, and compensation fixed at 80% of house value from an independent valuation. Vacated land stays in private ownership but is rezoned from building land to grassland. By January 2016, 146 of the 154 owners had received offers and 80 had accepted, and household exposure to flood risk had fallen by more than 50%. Coverage: one river basin area in Upper Austria. Access: the case study page, published on 7 April 2017 and modified on 25 August 2026, with Upper Austria's pages in German. Licence: Climate-ADAPT content under the EEA reuse policy; free. Caveats: the cost-benefit assessment is not public, the page states the budget in two ways, and figures stop in 2016. Simulation uses are parameterising managed retreat, uptake rates and exposure reduction in flood risk models. Related records: the Piemonte preventive relocation and Maasbommel case studies.
name: Voluntary relocation of flood-exposed households in the Eferdinger Becken, Upper Austria (Climate-ADAPT)
outcomes: After the 2002 and 2013 Danube floods, 154 properties were zoned for voluntary resettlement with compensation of 80% of house value; by January 2016, 146 owners had received offers and 80 had accepted, and household flood exposure had fallen by more than 50%.
